summary: This document specifies using the Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curve groups for key exchange in IKEv2.

eli5.summary: Two computers make a shared secret using math on special curves. This says they may use the Brainpool family of curves.

which brainpool curve should i use
subtitle: Using elliptic curve groups for secure key exchange

tldr.problem: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) needs additional options for elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) key exchange beyond those already standardized.
tldr.mechanism: This document registers four ECC Brainpool curve groups with specific Diffie-Hellman transform IDs (27-30) and specifies how to encode the key exchange payload and derive shared secrets using these curves.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 implementations can now use standardized Brainpool curves, which are ECC curves generated in a verifiably pseudo-random way and compliant with major cryptographic standards.

today: RFC 6954 is an Informational document that remains active. The Brainpool curves are now standardized options for IKEv2 key exchange and are implemented in modern cryptographic libraries and IPsec systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool curves are a standardized set of elliptic curve groups over finite prime fields. Defined in RFC 5639, these curves were generated in a verifiably pseudo-random way and comply with security requirements from ISO, ANSI, NIST, and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (SEC).

While RFC 5639 defined ASN.1 object identifiers for using Brainpool curves in certificates and certificate revocation lists, their use for key exchange in IKEv2 requires specific Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs in the IANA registry. This document provides those registrations and specifies the encoding and shared secret derivation methods.
sections.eli5: A math team created special curves that are good for secret codes. This document says how to use them with a standard protocol that computers use to swap secrets safely.

sections.title: Curve Registration and Transform IDs
sections.content:
Four specific Brainpool curves are registered for use in IKEv2 with the following Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs (Transform Type 4):

brainpoolP224r1 (Transform ID 27): A 224-bit curve offering 112 bits of symmetric strength. Each public value component (x and y coordinates) is 224 bits, making the complete key exchange payload 448 bits.

brainpoolP256r1 (Transform ID 28): A 256-bit curve offering 128 bits of symmetric strength, with 512-bit total payload.

brainpoolP384r1 (Transform ID 29): A 384-bit curve offering 192 bits of symmetric strength, with 768-bit total payload.

brainpoolP512r1 (Transform ID 30): A 512-bit curve offering 256 bits of symmetric strength, with 1024-bit total payload.

For performance optimization, implementations may use the twisted curve variant corresponding to each random curve, which offers the same security level but may allow more efficient arithmetic due to curve parameter A = -3. Public points can be efficiently transformed between the random and twisted curves using a quadratic twist transformation.
sections.eli5: Four different Brainpool curves with different sizes are available, numbered 27 through 30. Bigger curves give stronger codes but take longer to calculate.

sections.title: Key Exchange Payload and Shared Secret
sections.content:
The key exchange payload is constructed by concatenating the x and y coordinates of the public elliptic curve point. Each coordinate MUST be computed from the corresponding coordinate using the FieldElement-to-OctetString conversion method specified in SEC 1, with bit length as indicated for each curve. The conversion method enforces proper length by prepending zeros if necessary.

For the 256-bit curve (the most commonly used), each coordinate is 256 bits, resulting in a 512-bit key exchange payload. The 224-bit curve produces a 448-bit payload, the 384-bit curve produces a 768-bit payload, and the 512-bit curve produces a 1024-bit payload.

The Diffie-Hellman shared secret consists only of the x-coordinate of the computed shared point (not the y-coordinate). The x-coordinate MUST also be computed using the FieldElement-to-OctetString conversion method and have the bit length indicated for the curve (224, 256, 384, or 512 bits respectively).
sections.eli5: The key exchange sends two numbers (x and y) as the public code. The shared secret uses only the x number to save space and computation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations from RFC 5996 (IKEv2) apply fully to key exchange using Brainpool curves. A critical requirement is validation of the received peer's public Diffie-Hellman value: the x and y coordinates must be verified to satisfy the elliptic curve equation. This prevents certain active attacks.

The overall security of communications is limited by the weakest cryptographic primitive employed. When using Brainpool curves for key exchange, the following components should be chosen according to NIST 800-57 and RFC 5639 recommendations: the key derivation function, symmetric encryption algorithms and key lengths, and the algorithm, bit length, and hash function for signature generation.

Private Diffie-Hellman keys should be selected with the same bit length as the order of the group generated by the base point G and with approximately maximum entropy.

Implementations using the twisted curve variant internally should take particular care against side-channel attacks. Although the twisted curve offers the same security level as the random curve through mathematical equivalence, arithmetic based on small curve parameters (A = -3) may be harder to protect against side-channel attacks. General guidance on side-channel resistance is provided in standards from the Bundesamt fuer Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) and the "Guide to Elliptic Curve Cryptography".
sections.eli5: Make sure the numbers the other side sends actually work for the curve equation. Pick good random numbers for your secret, and match the curve size with other security choices.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered four Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs in the "Transform Type 4 - Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs" registry under the "Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) Parameters" namespace. The registrations are Transform ID 27 for brainpoolP224r1, ID 28 for brainpoolP256r1, ID 29 for brainpoolP384r1, and ID 30 for brainpoolP512r1.

These registrations enable interoperable use of Brainpool curves across different IKEv2 implementations. Any implementation claiming support for one of these transform IDs must follow the specifications in this document for encoding the key exchange payload and deriving the shared secret.
sections.eli5: The official IANA registry now lists these four curves as official choices that all IKEv2 systems can use.
